title: Qullamaggie Breakout and the Kell Cycle
teaches: The Qullamaggie breakout and Kell's cycle as we trade them: a leader rests 10 to 40 sessions in a tightening range with rising lows, surfing its rising averages, the buy is a market order as price trades over the base high, the stop sits a few cents under the breakout day's low and no wider than the ADR, a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail; Kell's cycle then says wait, buy, sell into strength or get out, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: An orderly pullback and consolidation with higher lows and tightening range in the consolidation phase.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: an orderly consolidation with higher lows and a tightening range.

facts.quote: During the consolidation the stock price “surfs” the rising 10- and 20-day.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: during the consolidation price surfs the rising 10- and 20-day.

facts.quote: just look at the daily chart and enter when the stock is starting to break out.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: on the daily chart, enter when the stock starts to break out.

facts.quote: This method can also be traded by anticipating the breakout but I don’t find it as effective and more skill and experience is needed.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: anticipating the breakout is less effective and needs more skill.

facts.quote: Stop is always lows of the day and stop should not be wider than the ATR or ADR of the stock
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day and no wider than the stock's ATR or ADR.

facts.quote: The rest of the position should be trailed with the 10- or the 20-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: trail the rest with the 10- or 20-day average.

facts.quote: 10 and 20-day exponential moving averages guide us through the intermediate-term trend
facts.claim: Kell: the 10 and 20-day EMAs guide the intermediate-term trend.

facts.quote: When the 10-day exponential moving average is below the 20-day, there is no reason to be long the stock.
facts.claim: Kell: with the 10-day EMA under the 20-day, there is no reason to be long.

facts.quote: The Reversal Extension is not necessarily a playable setup but more of a change in mindset.
facts.claim: Kell: the Reversal Extension is not necessarily a playable setup.

facts.quote: Many traders mistakenly believe the Wedge Pop is simply about crossing the moving averages.
facts.claim: Kell: a Wedge Pop is not simply a crossing of the averages.

facts.quote: Enter on a strong price bar with increased volume when the stock breaks through the pivot.
facts.claim: Kell: enter on a strong bar with increased volume through the pivot.

facts.quote: The EMA Crossback refers to the first time the stock price retests its moving averages after a strong upward move
facts.claim: Kell: the EMA Crossback is the first retest of the averages after a strong upward move.

facts.quote: But always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in before making your trade.
facts.claim: Kell: wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in.

facts.quote: The Base n’ Break is another pullback into the moving averages after the EMA Crossback.
facts.claim: Kell: the Base n' Break is another pullback into the averages after the EMA Crossback.

facts.quote: once you get two Base n’ Breaks, you should realize you are late in the intermediate-term cycle
facts.claim: Kell: after two Base n' Breaks you are late in the intermediate-term cycle.

facts.quote: The proper buy area is through the pivot into new highs.
facts.claim: Kell: the buy area is through the pivot into new highs.

facts.quote: The Exhaustion Extension is a euphoric blowoff price movement well above the 10-day moving average
facts.claim: Kell: the Exhaustion Extension is a blowoff well above the 10-day.

facts.quote: Start to get defensive when there is “air” between the low of the day and the 10EMA.
facts.claim: Kell: get defensive when there is air between the day's low and the 10 EMA.

facts.quote: The Wedge Drop happens when the market trades back below the moving averages after a strong rally, known as an Exhaustion Extension.
facts.claim: Kell: the Wedge Drop is a trade back below the averages after an Exhaustion Extension.

facts.quote: It may only be 3-4% above the moving averages but that was too much.
facts.claim: Kell, on his losers: 3-4% above the averages was too much.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first; the size comes from the stop; skip if the honest stop does not fit.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider.
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit and only moves up.

facts.quote: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account)
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R
facts.claim: B19: breakeven at 2R to 5R; the hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before earnings; hold through only if up 5R.

facts.quote: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day, unless it is a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups
facts.claim: C31: buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 10-day average for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.
facts.claim: E52: trail under the 10-day for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange A+ only; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: Grading a setup (A+, A, B, B-) is discretionary and hard to define
facts.claim: E50: grading a setup is discretionary and hard to define.

facts.quote: RS rating 80 or more.
facts.claim: Card: RS rating 80 or more.

facts.quote: On the breakout day the close is above the 50-day and the 200-day simple moving averages, with the 50-day above the 200-day.
facts.claim: Card: on the breakout day the close is above the 50-day and 200-day, with the 50 above the 200.

facts.quote: Record the stock's ADR, the 20-day average of high over low minus 1. No minimum is set; the ADR caps the stop.
facts.claim: Card: ADR is the 20-day average of high over low minus 1; it caps the stop.

facts.quote: Bull markets only: a Green market reading.
facts.claim: Card: bull markets only, a Green market reading.

facts.quote: The first base after the move is the A+ case; the second base or later is graded down, by analogy with Kell's count.
facts.claim: Card: the first base after the move is the A+ case.

facts.quote: A sideways consolidation after the move with at least two rising swing lows.
facts.claim: Card: a sideways consolidation with at least two rising swing lows.

facts.quote: The range tightens: the average daily range of the last 5 sessions is below the average of the whole consolidation.
facts.claim: Card: the last 5 sessions' average range is below the whole base's average.

facts.quote: The consolidation runs 10 to 40 sessions.
facts.claim: Card: the consolidation runs 10 to 40 sessions.

facts.quote: Consolidation high to low 25% or less, and no more than half of the prior move.
facts.claim: Card: base depth 25% or less, and no more than half of the prior move.

facts.quote: A consolidation 15% deep or less is the A+ depth.
facts.claim: Card: a base 15% deep or less is the A+ depth.

facts.quote: Through the consolidation, closes hold above the rising 20-day EMA; a brief undercut of the 20-day or a touch of the 50-day SMA is allowed.
facts.claim: Card: closes hold above the rising 20-day EMA through the base.

facts.quote: No volume rule. Lighter volume late in the base and heavier volume on the breakout raise the grade only.
facts.claim: Card: no volume rule; volume raises the grade only.

facts.quote: The daily-chart version: price trades above the consolidation high.
facts.claim: Card: the daily-chart version is a trade above the consolidation high.

facts.quote: A market order when the level breaks, set up from an alert placed the night before; regular hours only.
facts.claim: Card: a market order when the level breaks, from an alert set the night before.

facts.quote: No buy more than 4% above the trigger.
facts.claim: Card: no buy more than 4% above the trigger.

facts.quote: No anticipation inside the base. He allows it but finds it less effective and says more skill and experience is needed.
facts.claim: Card: no anticipation inside the base.

facts.quote: No new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report; hold through a report only if up 5R.
facts.claim: Card: no new buy in the 3 sessions before earnings.

facts.quote: A few cents under the low of the breakout day. At the moment of an opening-range buy that is the day's low so far, usually the opening-range low.
facts.claim: Card: a few cents under the breakout day's low, the day's low so far at an opening-range buy.

facts.quote: The stop must be no wider than the stock's ADR; if it is wider, skip.
facts.claim: Card: the stop must be no wider than the ADR; if wider, skip.

facts.quote: Sell a third at 3R.
facts.claim: Card: sell a third at 3R.

facts.quote: Trail the last third: a close under the 10-day for a fast mover, under the 21-day for a steadier one.
facts.claim: Card: trail the last third under the 10-day or 21-day, sold on a close.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop. The next flag in the same run is a new trade from flat, not an add.
facts.claim: Card: one price, one stop; the next flag in the same run is a new trade, not an add.

facts.quote: Before the trigger: a close under the consolidation low, or a close under the 50-day SMA, or a lower low inside the base.
facts.claim: Card: before the trigger, a close under the base low or the 50-day, or a lower low, ends it.

facts.quote: After the buy: a breakout that closes back inside the base in the lower third of its day's range is a failed breakout. Let the stop decide (the default) or sell on that close.
facts.claim: Card: a close back inside the base in the lower third of the day's range is a failed breakout; the stop decides.

facts.quote: a breakout that closes back inside the base in the lower third of its day's range is a failed breakout
facts.claim: Card: a close back inside the base in the lower third of the day's range is a failed breakout.

facts.quote: breaks early through the opening-range high and holds
facts.claim: Card, A+ cue: breaks early through the opening-range high and holds.

facts.quote: breaks late, closes off the high
facts.claim: Card, B- cue: breaks late, closes off the high.

facts.quote: the day's low well inside the ADR and within 3%
facts.claim: Card, A+ cue: the day's low well inside the ADR and within 3%.

facts.quote: RS 80 to 85, mid-pack in its group
facts.claim: Card, B- cue: RS 80 to 85, mid-pack in its group.

facts.quote: A flat base holds one box 15% deep or less for 25 sessions or more under a flat ceiling; Kullamagi's breakout rests 10 to 40 sessions with two or more rising swing lows, tightening at the end
facts.claim: Card: a flat base is one flat-topped box; the breakout rests with rising swing lows, tightening at the end.

facts.quote: A bull flag is a 3 to 15-session drift after a 20% pole; the Qullamaggie breakout is a 10 to 40-session consolidation. Under 10 sessions the rest is a flag
facts.claim: Card: under 10 sessions the rest is a bull flag; the breakout rests 10 to 40.

facts.quote: A wedge pop comes from under the 10 and 20 EMAs after a decline (8 or more of 15 closes under the 20 EMA); the Qullamaggie breakout's base surfs above the rising 20-day EMA the whole way
facts.claim: Card: a wedge pop comes from under the averages; the breakout's base surfs above the rising 20-day.

facts.quote: A crossback buys the first pullback into the rising 10 or 20 EMA after a pop, triggered over the prior day's high
facts.claim: Card: a crossback buys the first pullback into the rising 10 or 20 EMA after a pop.

facts.quote: One is a dip to a line, the other a new high.
facts.claim: Card: a crossback is a dip to a line, the breakout a new high.

facts.quote: where the stock sits against its 10 and 20-day EMAs decides whether to wait, buy, sell into strength or get out.
facts.claim: Card: where the stock sits against its 10 and 20-day EMAs decides whether to wait, buy, sell into strength or get out.

facts.quote: Up cycle: the 10 EMA above the 20 EMA, both rising. Down cycle: the 10 below the 20, both falling. No longs in a down cycle.
facts.claim: Card: an up cycle is the 10 EMA over the 20, both rising; no longs in a down cycle.

facts.quote: Air: the day's low is above the 10 EMA. Above both means a close above the 10 and the 20 EMA.
facts.claim: Card: air is the day's low above the 10 EMA.

facts.quote: Buying with air above the 10 EMA is a mistake; Kell found 3-4% above the averages too much.
facts.claim: Card: buying with air above the 10 EMA is a mistake.

facts.claim: Card: a Wedge Pop follows a Reversal Extension or a correction, with price and averages tightening.

facts.quote: Wedge Pop trigger: price trades through the pivot (the high of the tight range) and the day closes above both the 10 and 20 EMA, on volume at least the 50-day average; a gap up raises the grade.
facts.claim: Card: a Wedge Pop trades through the pivot and closes above both averages on volume at least the 50-day average.

facts.quote: A cross alone is not a Wedge Pop.
facts.claim: Card: a cross alone is not a Wedge Pop.

facts.quote: Wedge Pop stop: a few cents under the pop day's low, within the ADR and usually within about 3%; skip if it does not fit.
facts.claim: Card: the Wedge Pop stop is a few cents under the pop day's low, within the ADR.

facts.quote: the first pullback after the Wedge Pop that reaches the rising 10 or 20 EMA (the day's low within 1% of either, or an undercut of the 20 EMA that closes back above it)
facts.claim: Card: the Crossback is the first pullback after the Wedge Pop that reaches the rising 10 or 20 EMA.

facts.quote: moving sideways or drifting down gently, on volume below the 50-day average. The first one is A+.
facts.claim: Card: the Crossback drifts on volume below the 50-day average; the first one is A+.

facts.quote: EMA Crossback trigger: buyers show, price trades above the prior session's high.
facts.claim: Card: the Crossback trigger is a trade above the prior session's high.

facts.quote: EMA Crossback stop: a few cents under the pullback's low.
facts.claim: Card: the Crossback stop is a few cents under the pullback's low.

facts.quote: Base n' Break setting: in an up cycle, near the highs, a tight base of 5 to 15 sessions (1 to 3 weeks) whose lows hold the rising 10/20 EMA.
facts.claim: Card: a Base n' Break is a tight base of 5 to 15 sessions holding the rising 10/20 EMA.

facts.quote: The first Base n' Break is normal. From the second on, the stock is late in its cycle: grade down, sell into strength sooner and watch for an Exhaustion Extension.
facts.claim: Card: from the second Base n' Break on, the stock is late in its cycle; grade down.

facts.quote: for a stock, a close 10% or more above the 10-day
facts.claim: Card: for a stock, an Exhaustion Extension is a close 10% or more above the 10-day.

facts.quote: Exhaustion Extension: air (the day's low above the 10 EMA) and a close far above the 10 EMA
facts.claim: Card: an Exhaustion Extension is air and a close far above the 10 EMA.

facts.quote: Count the extensions: after 3 to 4 of them, expect a longer base.
facts.claim: Card: after 3 to 4 extensions, expect a longer base.

facts.quote: price trades tight into the averages and then closes below both the 10 and 20 EMA, on volume above the 50-day average
facts.claim: Card: a Wedge Drop trades tight into the averages and closes below both on volume above the 50-day average.

facts.quote: For longs, the house trail already exits on a Wedge Drop: a close under the 10-day or 21-day. Holding through a Wedge Drop is a mistake.
facts.claim: Card: for longs, the trail already exits on a Wedge Drop; holding through it is a mistake.

facts.quote: Fewer trades and lower exposure when the index is below its 20 EMA.
facts.claim: Card: fewer trades and lower exposure when the index is below its 20 EMA.

steps: CRSP, 2019. A 47% run begins on an earnings reaction, then the stock rests 10 sessions in a 14% band.
The base checks out: 10 sessions is the shortest allowed, and 14% is inside the 25% depth cap.
2019-11-12: it clears 52.28 on 3.1x volume. Buy at market, 52.35. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 51.21.
The stop is 2.2%, inside the 5.6% ADR. Failure mode: a close back inside the base. Instead 3R came in 1 day.

walkthroughs.title: HWM, May 2025: a steady name after an earnings gap

questions.q: What shape does the base take before a Qullamaggie breakout?
choices: Sideways, higher lows, tight range
Sideways, lower lows, widening range
Sideways, flat lows, wide swings
Drifting down through the 20-day
questions.answer: Sideways, higher lows, tight range
questions.why: Sideways, with higher lows and a tightening range. Kullamagi calls it an orderly consolidation with higher lows and a tightening range. UCT's card asks for a sideways consolidation after the move with at least two rising swing lows. Lower lows, wide swings or a drift under the 20-day are not this base.
questions.lesson_line: Rest, don't fall: higher lows and a tighter range into the break.

wrong.Sideways, lower lows, widening range: The card needs at least two rising swing lows, and a range that tightens, not one that widens.
wrong.Sideways, flat lows, wide swings: Kullamagi wants higher lows and a tightening range. Flat lows with wide swings are neither.
wrong.Drifting down through the 20-day: The base surfs the rising 10- and 20-day, and closes hold above the rising 20-day.

questions.simple: The base is a calm sideways rest where the lows keep rising and the daily range gets tighter.

reasons: Two agreeing facts: Kullamagi's page and UCT's card

questions.q: The breakout is for leaders: stocks with an RS rating of 80 or more.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. Kullamagi scans for the 1 or 2% of stocks up the most over three timeframes.
questions.lesson_line: Breakouts are for leaders. Check the RS rating first.
questions.simple: True, because we buy leaders, and a leader has an RS rating of 80 or more.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On the breakout day our card wants the close above the 50-day and ___-day simple averages.
questions.why: 200. On the breakout day the close is above the 50-day and the 200-day, with the 50-day above the 200-day. Our rule is no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 50, above the 200, and the 50 over the 200.
questions.simple: The close must be above the 50-day and 200-day averages, with the 50-day above the 200-day.

deeper.trap: Two ideas sit in this one line. No longs below the 200-day simple average is the rulebook line, with one exception, a parabolic long. The 50-day above the 200-day is how the card reads a leader's stack. Mixing them up makes the rule sound stricter or looser than it is.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
the 50-over-200 half is the card's reading, not the rulebook's

questions.q: On the daily chart, how is the breakout bought?
choices: With a limit order just above the high
At market as it clears the base high
Half at the break, half on the retest
At market after a close above the high
questions.answer: At market as it clears the base high
questions.why: At market as price trades over the base high. This is the daily-chart version: Kullamagi says to enter when the stock starts to break out. Our entries are market orders, set up from an alert the night before, in regular hours only.
questions.lesson_line: Price trades over the base high, and you buy at market.

wrong.With a limit order just above the high: Our entries are market orders, bought as the level breaks.
wrong.Half at the break, half on the retest: We buy the full size at one price with one stop. The next flag in the same run is a new trade, not an add.
wrong.At market after a close above the high: The card buys with a market order when the level breaks. It does not wait for a close above it.

questions.simple: You buy at market the moment price trades over the base high, so you catch the break as it starts.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, market orders)

questions.q: The stop sits a few cents under the breakout day's low.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The stop sits a few cents under the breakout day's low, not exactly on it. Kullamagi: the stop is always the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the breakout day's low.
questions.simple: True, the stop goes a few cents under the breakout day's low, not right on it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F62, A4)

questions.q: The stop may be wider than the stock's ADR if the chart is clean.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The stop must be no wider than the stock's ADR, and if it is wider, skip the trade. ADR is the 20-day average of high over low minus 1. Kullamagi says the same of the stock's ATR or ADR. A clean chart does not widen the limit.
questions.lesson_line: A stop wider than the ADR is a skip, however clean the chart.
questions.simple: False, because a stop wider than the stock's average daily range means you skip the trade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3)
one web quote plus the card

questions.q: Per Kullamagi, which lines does the stock 'surf' during the base?
choices: The falling 50- and 200-day averages
The 100- and 150-day averages
The rising 10- and 20-day averages
The rising 50- and 100-day averages
questions.answer: The rising 10- and 20-day averages
questions.why: The rising 10- and 20-day averages. Kullamagi: during the consolidation the stock surfs the rising 10- and 20-day. Our card reads it as closes holding above the rising 20-day EMA. A brief undercut of the 20-day or a touch of the 50-day is allowed. He does not say whether the averages are EMA or SMA.
questions.lesson_line: A good base surfs the rising 10- and 20-day.

wrong.The falling 50- and 200-day averages: He says the stock surfs the rising 10- and 20-day. Falling averages are not his line.
wrong.The 100- and 150-day averages: He says the stock surfs the rising 10- and 20-day, not the 100- or 150-day.
wrong.The rising 50- and 100-day averages: He names the rising 10- and 20-day as the lines the stock surfs.

questions.simple: The stock surfs the rising 10- and 20-day averages while it rests.

reasons: averages are the card's proposed reading, EMA or SMA unstated by the source

questions.q: How many sessions does a Qullamaggie base rest?
choices: 3 to 15 sessions
10 to 40 sessions
Over 40 sessions
5 to 15 sessions
questions.answer: 10 to 40 sessions
questions.why: 10 to 40 sessions. UCT's card says the consolidation runs 10 to 40 sessions. Kullamagi says usually 2 weeks to 2 months, which is close. Under 10 sessions the rest is a flag, not this base.
questions.lesson_line: Ten to forty sessions of rest, not a few days and not a season.

wrong.3 to 15 sessions: That is the bull flag's drift after a 20% pole, not this base.
wrong.Over 40 sessions: That is longer than the card allows. The consolidation runs 10 to 40 sessions.
wrong.5 to 15 sessions: That is the Base n' Break's tight base, a different phase.

questions.simple: The rest runs 10 to 40 sessions, close to the 2 weeks to 2 months Kullamagi gives.

reasons: A session count that is the card's own proposed number
Fixed before

questions.q: On our card, what is the deepest a base may be, high to low?
questions.why: 25%, measured from the consolidation high to its low, and no more than half of the prior move. A base 15% deep or less is the A+ depth.
questions.lesson_line: Shallow bases are stronger. Past 25% deep it is no longer this base.

wrong.15%: 15% is the A+ depth, not the limit. The cap is 25%.
wrong.10%: The card sets no 10% limit. The cap is 25%.
wrong.50%: That is far past the cap. The card allows 25%.

questions.simple: The base can be at most 25% deep, and the shallower it is the better.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (held)
the 25% cap is the card's proposed number and the owner has not ruled on it
a number that may change

questions.q: The card says breakouts are for bull markets only. Which market reading is that?
choices: Green
Yellow
Orange
Red
questions.answer: Green
questions.why: Green. The card says bull markets only, a Green market reading. Green is full risk per grade and up to 10 positions. Yellow is smaller and fewer, Orange is A+ setups only, and Red is mostly cash and shorts.
questions.lesson_line: On our card, bull markets only means a Green reading.

wrong.Yellow: Yellow means smaller and fewer. The card names Green for bull markets.
wrong.Orange: Orange means only A+ setups. The card names Green for bull markets.
wrong.Red: Red means mostly cash and shorts. The card names Green for bull markets.

questions.simple: The card's line, bull markets only, names a Green market reading.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)
the card says Green only while the rulebook lets Yellow trade smaller

questions.q: Our Qullamaggie breakout rule sets a minimum volume on the breakout day.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. There is no volume rule for this breakout. Lighter volume late in the base and heavier volume on the breakout raise the grade only. A breakout on 0.7x volume still worked in our data.
questions.lesson_line: Volume raises the grade. It is not a gate.
questions.simple: False, because volume only raises the grade and is never a gate you must pass.

reasons: rests on the criteria card, which the owner has not yet ruled on

questions.q: Which base after the big move does our card grade highest?
choices: The first base after the move
The second base after the move
The third base after the move
The deepest base on the chart
questions.answer: The first base after the move
questions.why: The first base after the move. On our card the first base is the A+ case, and the second base or later is graded down. The card sets this by analogy with Kell's count. Graded down means a lower grade, not a ban. Grading stays a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: First base after the move is the best one.

wrong.The third base after the move: A second base or later is graded down, and a third is later still.
wrong.The second base after the move: A second base or later is graded down.
wrong.The deepest base on the chart: A base 15% deep or less is the A+ depth, so a deeper base is not the best case.

questions.simple: The first base after the big move is the best one, because later bases are graded down.

reasons: The count rule is the card's own, built by analogy with Kell

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: ADR is the 20-day average of high over low, minus ___.
questions.why: 1. ADR is the 20-day average of high over low, minus 1. That gives the stock's average daily range as a fraction. The stop must be no wider than the ADR, and if it is wider we skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: ADR caps the stop. Know the stock's ADR before you buy.
questions.simple: ADR is each day's high divided by its low, averaged, minus 1, so it shows the usual daily swing.

reasons: rests on the criteria card, which the owner has not yet ruled on

questions.q: Bought at 161.59 with the stop at 158.95. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 169.51. One R is the buy minus the stop. Three R is the buy of 161.59 plus three of those. The first third comes off there. HWM got there in 7 days.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.
questions.simple: One R is the buy minus the stop, so add three of those to the buy to find 3R.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: The base high is 64.40 and the base low is 52.10. How deep is it, in percent of the high, to one decimal?
questions.why: 19.1. Depth is the drop from the base high to the base low, over the base high. Take 64.40 minus 52.10, divide by 64.40, and round to one decimal. That is inside the 25% cap but deeper than the 15% A+ depth.
questions.lesson_line: Depth in percent of the base high. Under 15% is the A+ depth.
questions.simple: Take the drop from the base high to the base low and divide by the high to get 19.1 percent.

deeper.trap: Divide by the base high, not the base low. The card measures depth as the consolidation high minus its low, over the high. Dividing by the low gives a bigger number and can push a good base past the cap.

reasons: a computed key
the 25% cap named in the explanation is the card's proposed number

questions.q: On an opening-range buy, where does the stop go?
choices: Under the 20-day moving average
A few cents under the base low
10% under the price you paid
A few cents under the day's low
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the day's low so far, usually the opening-range low. At the moment of an opening-range buy, the breakout day's low is the low so far. The stop sits a few cents under it, not exactly on it, and no wider than the stock's ADR.
questions.lesson_line: On the first buy, the day's low so far is the stop.

wrong.Under the 20-day moving average: A stop under the average instead of the day's low is a listed mistake.
wrong.A few cents under the base low: The card puts the stop under the breakout day's low, not the base low.
wrong.10% under the price you paid: A fixed percent ignores the chart and can break the ADR cap.

questions.simple: The stop goes a few cents under the low of the day so far, which is usually the opening-range low.

deeper.trap: A stop under a moving average looks safer, but it ignores the breakout day's low. The stop must also be no wider than the stock's ADR. If it is wider, skip the trade.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (F62)
Opening-range version is the card's; the examples tested only the daily-chart trigger

questions.q: How close to an earnings report may we buy a breakout?
choices: Not within 3 sessions before
Any time; the chart decides
Not within 10 sessions before
Not within 2 sessions before
questions.answer: Not within 3 sessions before
questions.why: Not within the 3 sessions before a report. We hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. The risk is a report that gaps the stock through the stop.
questions.lesson_line: No new buy in the 3 sessions before a report.

wrong.Any time; the chart decides: A report inside the window can gap the stock through the stop.
wrong.Not within 10 sessions before: That is longer than the rule. The rule is 3 sessions before.
wrong.Not within 2 sessions before: That is shorter than the rule. A buy 3 sessions before a report is already inside it.

questions.simple: Do not buy in the 3 sessions before earnings, because a report can gap the stock through your stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: What does 'tightening' mean on our card?
choices: Last 5 days range less than the base
Last 5 days volume less than the base
The base is 15% deep or less
The 10 and 20-day move closer together
questions.answer: Last 5 days range less than the base
questions.why: The average daily range of the last 5 sessions is below the average of the whole consolidation. Tightening is about daily range near the end of the base. It is not depth, not volume and not a shorter base.
questions.lesson_line: A tight finish: the last 5 sessions range less than the base average.

wrong.Last 5 days volume less than the base: Volume is not part of the tightening test. The card has no volume rule, and volume only raises the grade.
wrong.The base is 15% deep or less: That is the A+ depth, a different test from tightening.
wrong.The 10 and 20-day move closer together: Averages that converge belong to the Wedge Pop setting, not to this test.

questions.simple: Tightening means the daily range over the last 5 sessions is smaller than the average range of the whole base.

reasons: Only the card states the 5-session test
A number from the card's proposed criteria
Fixed before

questions.q: You may buy a strong breakout 6% above the trigger.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The card says no buy more than 4% above the trigger. The rulebook says never buy more than 4% above the buy point. At 6% past it you are chasing, however strong the breakout. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% past the trigger is a chase. Skip it.
questions.simple: No, 6% past the trigger is too far. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, the 4% limit)

questions.q: Kullamagi trails the rest of the position with the 10- or 20-day average.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Kullamagi trails the rest with the 10- or the 20-day moving average. Ours is nearly the same line: a close under the 10-day for fast movers, or under the 21-day for steadier ones. In our plan the rest is the last third, after the trims at 3R and 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the last third under the 10-day or 21-day.
questions.simple: Yes. He trails the rest with the 10- or 20-day average, and we use a close under the 10-day or 21-day.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (E52, the trail)

questions.q: The EMA Crossback is bought as price trades above the prior session's high.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Buyers show when price trades above the prior session's high on the first pullback into the rising averages. Kell says to always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in. The stop sits a few cents under the pullback's low.
questions.lesson_line: Wait for buyers: the Crossback buys over the prior session's high.
questions.simple: Yes. You wait for buyers to show by trading above the prior day's high, not just for a dip to the averages.

reasons: The trigger is the card's reading of Kell's confirmation

questions.q: Buy at market, or pass?
choices: Buy; this breakout is clearly real
Pass; it is over 4% above the high
Buy half now and half on a dip
Buy; it is under the 10% stretch limit
questions.answer: Pass; it is over 4% above the high
questions.why: Pass. The base high is 77.67 and we never buy more than 4% above the buy point. At 81.20 the stock is more than 4% above it. A real breakout bought that far past the trigger is a chase, so we skip it rather than scale in. The 10% limit above the 10-day average is a separate test.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% past the trigger, skip it.

wrong.Buy; this breakout is clearly real: A real breakout bought more than 4% past the trigger is a chase.
wrong.Buy half now and half on a dip: No scaling. The price is past the limit and the plan skips it.
wrong.Buy; it is under the 10% stretch limit: The 10% line is a separate test for a long stretched above its 10-day. The 4% limit above the buy point still applies.

questions.story: The base high is 77.67. At 10:05 the stock trades at 81.20, and the trigger has long passed.
questions.simple: Pass, because the price is already more than 4% above the base high and that is chasing.

deeper.counter: Passing today is not a ban on the stock. A missed breakout that comes back to the breakout level may be bought as a new trade with its own trigger and stop. What the plan forbids is buying more than 4% above the buy point.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

questions.q: Prior move 35.00 to 52.28. Base high 52.28, base low 45.00. What share of the move did it give back, in percent?
questions.why: 42.1. The drop from 52.28 to 45.00, divided by the move from 35.00 to 52.28, is 42.1%. The cap is no more than half of the prior move, so it passes.
questions.lesson_line: Give-back as a share of the move. Half is the most.
questions.simple: The base gave back 42.1 percent of the move, which is under half, so it passes the cap.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the criteria card, which the owner has not yet ruled on
one cited fact only

questions.q: Buy the break?
choices: Yes; the volume confirms it
Yes, with half size
No; a report is within 3 sessions
questions.answer: No; a report is within 3 sessions
questions.why: No. No new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report. Check the report date before you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date first. A gap through the stop is not planned risk.

wrong.Yes; the volume confirms it: Volume does not move the earnings rule. No new buy in the 3 sessions before.
wrong.Yes, with half size: Half size does not fix a gap through the stop.

questions.q: What do you do with the stop?
choices: Keep it; the stop decides
Lower it to give the trade room
Add more at the lower price
questions.answer: Keep it; the stop decides
questions.why: Keep it. A close back inside the base in the lower third of its range is a failed breakout, and the stop decides.
questions.lesson_line: A failed close is a warning. The stop stays where it was.

wrong.Lower it to give the trade room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Add more at the lower price: No adds. One price, one stop.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 38.01 with the stop at 37.37. It closes at 37.60, back inside the base in the bottom third of its range.

questions.q: Buying inside the base, before it breaks, is the standard entry.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The standard entry is the trade through the base high, not a buy inside the base. Kullamagi says anticipating the breakout is less effective and needs more skill and experience. Our card goes further: no anticipation inside the base.
questions.lesson_line: Wait for the trade through the level. Anticipating is harder.
questions.simple: No, you wait for price to trade over the base high. Buying early is harder and less effective.

reasons: Our card is stricter than the originator, who allows anticipating

questions.q: Take the trade?

No; the stop is beyond the ADR

wrong.Yes, if you take a smaller size: The stop may not be wider than the ADR. Over it, we skip, whatever the size.
wrong.Yes, if you move the stop to 4.0%: The stop is the honest stop under the day's low. If it does not fit, skip the trade; do not pull it in.
wrong.No; a 4.0% ADR is too low to trade: No ADR minimum is set. The ADR only caps the stop.

questions.story: A stock's ADR is 4.0%. The breakout day's low sits 5.5% under your buy.

questions.q: Flat Base or Qullamaggie breakout?
choices: Flat Base; 25 sessions is its length
Qullamaggie breakout; not a flat box
Bull Flag; it paused after a big run
Neither; 25 sessions is too long
questions.answer: Qullamaggie breakout; not a flat box
questions.why: Qullamaggie breakout. It rests 10 to 40 sessions with rising swing lows, tightening at the end, and 25 sessions is inside that. A flat base is one flat-topped box, so the shape of the lows tells them apart, not the length. A bull flag is a short drift, so 25 sessions is too long for it.
questions.lesson_line: Check the lows. Rising lows and a tight finish mean this breakout.

wrong.Neither; 25 sessions is too long: Twenty-five sessions is inside the 10 to 40 range.
wrong.Flat Base; 25 sessions is its length: A flat base is one flat-topped box 15% deep or less. Rising swing lows are not one box.
wrong.Bull Flag; it paused after a big run: A bull flag is a 3 to 15-session drift after a 20% pole. Twenty-five sessions is far too long for that.

questions.story: A leader rests 25 sessions after a big run. Its swing lows keep rising, and the range tightens at the end.
questions.simple: The lows rise and the range tightens, so it is the breakout and not a flat box under a flat ceiling.

deeper.counter: The length does not tell a flat base from this breakout, since 25 sessions fits both. The tell is the shape of the lows. A flat base sits in one box under a flat ceiling. This base has lows that keep rising and a range that tightens at the end.

reasons: Compares against Flat Base and Bull Flag; the setup map is held (D-002)
Cut-offs come from the card's proposed criteria

questions.q: Bull Flag or Qullamaggie breakout?
choices: Bull Flag; five sessions, under 10
Qullamaggie breakout; it ran up 45%
Neither; the drift is too short
Wedge Pop; it drifted after the run
questions.answer: Bull Flag; five sessions, under 10
questions.why: Bull Flag. A bull flag is a 3 to 15-session drift after a 20% pole, and this rest is five sessions. The Qullamaggie breakout rests 10 to 40 sessions, so under 10 sessions the rest is a flag. The 45% run alone does not decide it.
questions.lesson_line: Count the sessions. Under 10 is a flag.

wrong.Qullamaggie breakout; it ran up 45%: The run alone does not decide it. Under 10 sessions the rest is a flag.
wrong.Neither; the drift is too short: A short tight rest after a pole is a flag, a named setup of its own.
wrong.Wedge Pop; it drifted after the run: A Wedge Pop follows a Reversal Extension or a correction of 15% or more. This stock ran up and then drifted.

questions.story: A stock runs 45%, then drifts sideways for five sessions.
questions.simple: A five-session rest is shorter than 10 sessions, so it is a flag and not this breakout.

reasons: Compares against Bull Flag; the setup map is held (D-002)
Numbers from the card's proposed criteria

questions.q: Which setup does this look like?
choices: Breakout; it cleared the range
Wedge Pop; the base sat below its EMAs
Base n' Break; it is near its high
EMA Crossback; it is retesting the 20
questions.answer: Wedge Pop; the base sat below its EMAs
questions.why: Wedge Pop. A wedge pop comes from under the 10 and 20 EMAs after a decline. The card's mark is 8 or more of 15 closes under the 20 EMA. This stock had 11 of 15. The breakout's base surfs above the rising 20-day the whole way. Clearing the range does not tell the two apart.
questions.lesson_line: Check where the base sat against the averages. Under them means a wedge pop.

wrong.Breakout; it cleared the range: The breakout's base surfs above the rising 20-day the whole way.
wrong.Base n' Break; it is near its high: A Base n' Break needs lows holding the rising 10/20 EMA.
wrong.EMA Crossback; it is retesting the 20: A Crossback is a dip to a line after a pop. This stock spent most of its closes under the 20 EMA first.

questions.story: A stock spent 11 of its last 15 closes under its 20 EMA. Today it pushes through the top of its range.
questions.simple: Most of its recent closes sat under the 20 EMA, so this is a wedge pop and not a breakout.

reasons: The 8-of-15 count is the card's own proposed number

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: Qullamaggie breakout
Base n' Break
EMA Crossback
Wedge Pop
questions.answer: EMA Crossback
questions.why: EMA Crossback. It buys the first pullback into the rising 10 or 20 EMA after a pop, triggered over the prior day's high. A crossback is a dip to a line, while the breakout is a new high out of a base. This stock popped, dipped to its rising 20 EMA for the first time and turned up.
questions.lesson_line: A dip to a line is a crossback. A new high out of a base is the breakout.

wrong.Qullamaggie breakout: The breakout buys a new high out of a base. A crossback buys a dip to a line.
wrong.Base n' Break: A Base n' Break is another pullback into the averages after the EMA Crossback. This is the first dip.
wrong.Wedge Pop: A Wedge Pop comes from under the 10 and 20 EMAs after a decline. This stock popped first, then dipped to its rising 20 EMA.

questions.story: A stock popped, then dipped to its rising 20 EMA for the first time and turned up. You buy over the prior day's high.
questions.simple: It is an EMA Crossback, because the stock popped and then dipped to its rising 20 EMA for the first time.

reasons: card criterion for Kell's crossback, constructed story

questions.q: What is the only thing the volume changes on these two breakouts?
choices: The breakout's grade
The breakout's validity
The stop's maximum width
The base's tightness
questions.answer: The breakout's grade
questions.why: Only the grade. The card has no volume rule. Lighter volume late in the base and heavier volume on the breakout raise the grade, nothing else. ISRG broke out of a 13%-deep flag on 0.7x volume and still worked. CPRI broke on 0.8x volume and reached 3R in 5 days.
questions.lesson_line: Volume moves the grade, not the verdict.

wrong.The breakout's validity: There is no volume rule, so neither breakout is invalid for its volume.
wrong.The stop's maximum width: The stop is the day's low and capped by ADR, not by volume.
wrong.The base's tightness: Tight means the range narrows: the last 5 sessions' average range sits below the whole base's, whatever the volume.

questions.story: Two breakouts of the same base: one on 0.7x volume, one on 3.1x.
questions.simple: Volume only changes the grade, because the card has no volume rule.

deeper.counter: Heavy volume is still welcome: it raises the grade. The mistake is skipping a quiet breakout as invalid. ISRG on 0.7x volume and CPRI on 0.8x volume both worked, though two examples do not make a rate.

reasons: the card's volume line is a proposed criterion
two examples, not a rate

questions.q: Using our card's grade cues, how do the two breakout days compare?
choices: Day A grades higher
Day B grades higher
They grade the same
Neither can be graded
questions.answer: Day A grades higher
questions.why: Day A grades higher. Breaking early through the opening-range high and holding is an A+ cue. Breaking late and closing off the high is a B- cue. These are cues, not a checklist: grading a setup is discretionary and hard to define.
questions.lesson_line: Early and holding grades well. Late and off the high does not.

wrong.Day B grades higher: Breaking late and closing off the high is a B- cue.
wrong.They grade the same: The card treats the early break that holds as an A+ cue and the late break off the high as a B- cue.
wrong.Neither can be graded: The card lists both breakout days among its grade cues.

questions.story: Two breakouts from similar bases. Day A breaks early through the opening-range high and holds. Day B breaks late and closes off the high.
questions.simple: Day A grades higher, because breaking early through the opening-range high and holding is an A+ cue.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E50)
grade cues on the card are proposed

questions.q: Does that stop help the grade?
choices: No; a very tight stop is a weak sign
No; only the ADR matters
Yes; inside the ADR and within 3%
Yes, and it alone makes it an A+
questions.answer: Yes; inside the ADR and within 3%
questions.why: Yes. The day's low well inside the ADR and within 3% is an A+ cue. HWM's stop was 1.6% under a 2.9% ADR, so it fits both tests. It is one cue, not the whole grade: grading a setup is discretionary and hard to define.
questions.lesson_line: A stop well inside the ADR and under 3% is a good sign.

wrong.No; a very tight stop is a weak sign: A day's low well inside the ADR and within 3% is an A+ cue.
wrong.No; only the ADR matters: The cue needs both: well inside the ADR and within 3%.
wrong.Yes, and it alone makes it an A+: It is one A+ cue, not the whole grade. Grading a setup is discretionary and hard to define.

questions.story: HWM, 2025. The stop sits 1.6% under the entry and the stock's ADR is 2.9%.
questions.simple: Yes, a stop well inside the ADR and within 3% is an A+ cue, and 1.6% fits both.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A13, E50)

questions.q: How does the card read that?
choices: Passes the rule; reads as a B- cue
Fails the rule; 82 is below the line
Passes the rule; reads as an A+ cue
Fails the rule; it needs RS 90 or more
questions.answer: Passes the rule; reads as a B- cue
questions.why: It passes the rule and reads as a B- cue. The rule is an RS rating of 80 or more, and 82 meets it. RS 80 to 85, mid-pack in its group, is a B- cue. Grading stays a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: Pass the 80 line, but a mid-pack leader grades lower.

wrong.Fails the rule; 82 is below the line: The rule is RS 80 or more, so 82 passes.
wrong.Passes the rule; reads as an A+ cue: RS 90 or more, or a top-2% gainer, is the A+ cue. RS 80 to 85, mid-pack in its group, is a B- cue.
wrong.Fails the rule; it needs RS 90 or more: The rule is RS 80 or more. RS 90 or more is an A+ cue, not the pass line.

questions.story: A breakout candidate has an RS rating of 82 and is mid-pack in its group.
questions.simple: 82 clears the 80 line, but a mid-pack leader reads as a B- cue, below a top one.

Grade cues are the card's proposed bands

questions.q: Is the second break an add or a new trade?
choices: An add to the first trade
A new trade from flat, not an add
Skip it; a run gets one trade
A new trade that keeps the old stop
questions.answer: A new trade from flat, not an add
questions.why: A new trade from flat, not an add. The next flag in the same run gets its own trigger, stop and size. We hold the full size at one price with one stop and never add. MSTR's next flag in the same run is the example.
questions.lesson_line: Each flag is its own trade. Never an add.

wrong.An add to the first trade: The first trade is over, and we never add. One price, one stop.
wrong.Skip it; a run gets one trade: The next flag in the same run is its own trade, from flat.
wrong.A new trade that keeps the old stop: Each trade has its own stop and size. The next flag in the same run is a new trade from flat.

questions.story: A stock broke out, ran, and you sold your shares. Weeks later it rests in a new flag in the same run. It breaks out again.
questions.simple: It is a new trade with its own stop, not an add, because we never add to a position.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)

questions.q: Is that 10-session rest long enough for a Qullamaggie base?
choices: No; it needs at least 20 sessions
No; a 14% band is too deep for a base
Yes; it is the shortest rest allowed
Yes; a big run excuses a short rest
questions.answer: Yes; it is the shortest rest allowed
questions.why: Yes. The base runs 10 to 40 sessions, and CRSP's 10 sessions is the shortest allowed. Its 14% depth is inside the 25% cap, and the 47% run came first. Volume does not decide it, since the card has no volume rule. 3R came in 1 day after the break on 3.1x volume.
questions.lesson_line: Ten sessions is the shortest base that counts.

wrong.No; it needs at least 20 sessions: The base runs 10 to 40 sessions. Ten is the shortest.
wrong.No; a 14% band is too deep for a base: A base 25% deep or less qualifies, and 14% is inside it.
wrong.Yes; a big run excuses a short rest: The rest length is its own rule, 10 to 40 sessions. The size of the run does not change it.

questions.story: CRSP, 2019. After a 47% run, the stock rests 10 sessions in a 14% band, then breaks out on 3.1x volume.
questions.simple: Yes, 10 sessions is the shortest rest allowed, and CRSP's 14% depth is well inside the 25% cap.

deeper.example: CRSP rested 10 sessions in a 14% band and broke out on 3.1x volume. CPRI broke out on 0.8x volume, and ISRG on 0.7x, and both still worked. That is why the card makes volume a grade, not a rule.

reasons: Example read from the research scan, not reviewed by the owner
Session and depth limits are the card's proposed numbers

questions.q: Does that 22% depth pass our card's depth rule?
choices: Yes; 22% is under the 25% cap
No; 22% is over the 15% line
No; 22% is over half the 71% run
Yes; a 71% run excuses any depth
questions.answer: Yes; 22% is under the 25% cap
questions.why: Yes. The depth cap is 25% or less, high to low, and 22% is under it. It also stays under half of the 71% run, the second cap. The 37 sessions are inside 10 to 40. It passes the cap but is not the A+ depth, which is 15% or less. Grading stays a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: Under 25% passes. Under 15% is the A+ depth.

wrong.No; 22% is over the 15% line: Fifteen percent is the A+ depth, not the cap. A base can pass the cap without it.
wrong.No; 22% is over half the 71% run: The card allows up to half of the prior move. 22% is well under half of a 71% run.
wrong.Yes; a 71% run excuses any depth: The cap is 25% or less however big the run. A bigger run does not excuse a deeper base.

questions.story: AMD, 2000. A 71% run, then a 37-session shelf 22% deep, surfing the rising 10- and 20-day. The stock breaks out on 1.9x volume.
questions.simple: 22% is under the 25% cap, so the base passes, though it is not the 15% A+ depth.

deeper.trap: Two caps apply: 25% or less, and no more than half of the prior move. AMD's 22% passes both, since half of its 71% run is more than 22%. Passing the cap is not the same as the A+ depth, which needs 15% or less.

reasons: The 25% cap is proposed and the owner's own MRAM base ran deeper
Example read from the research scan

questions.q: Was the loss a rule break?
choices: Yes; you should have held through
No; late base, and the stop worked
No; but a late base should be skipped
Yes; you should have trimmed at 2R
questions.answer: No; late base, and the stop worked
questions.why: No. NVDA was a late base, far along its yearly advance, which is Kell's late-in-the-cycle case. The base fits 10 to 40 sessions, the buy at 144.43 had its stop at 141.91 (1.7%), and the stop did its job on day 7. It reached 2.12R but never 3R, where the first trim is a third.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out with the rules followed is a planned loss.

wrong.Yes; you should have held through: The stop is the exit. Holding through it breaks the rule.
wrong.No; but a late base should be skipped: A late stock is graded down and sold into strength sooner. The card does not skip it.
wrong.Yes; you should have trimmed at 2R: The first trim is a third at 3R. The trade reached 2.12R and never got there.

questions.story: NVDA, 2024. A 23-session base after a 32% run breaks out, and the stock is far along its yearly advance. You buy at 144.43 with the stop at 141.91. It reaches 2.12R, then is stopped on day 7.
questions.simple: No, because it was a late base and the stop did its job, so no rule was broken.

deeper.counter: Breakeven is the other lens. Moving the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R is the ideal, and NVDA passed 2R, so that stop would have ended it at breakeven. But ideally is not a hard rule. The hard rules are the stop and a third off at 3R, and both were followed.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B19)
late-base grading rests on a proposed card line
a number-heavy walk

questions.q: Which rule would have kept you out?
choices: No buy over 4% above the trigger
Stop no wider than the stock's ADR
No buy 3 sessions before a report
Let a gap's first 30 minutes decide
questions.answer: No buy 3 sessions before a report
questions.why: No buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report. The report came that evening and the next day gapped to a low of 112.91, through the 119.75 stop. The buy date was the mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date first, then the chart.

wrong.No buy over 4% above the trigger: That rule limits how far above the trigger you buy. This story is about a report that came that evening.
wrong.Stop no wider than the stock's ADR: That rule limits how wide the stop is. It does not keep you out ahead of a report.
wrong.Let a gap's first 30 minutes decide: That rule manages a gap after you own the stock. It does not keep you out of the buy.

questions.story: AMZN, 2020 (prices split-adjusted). A base breaks out. You buy at 123.06. The report comes that evening and the next day gaps below your 119.75 stop.
questions.simple: Our rule bars new buys in the 3 sessions before a report, and this buy came the day of one.

deeper.trap: This was not a normal stop-out. The next day gapped to a low of 112.91, below the 119.75 stop, and the trade never traded above the entry. Here the gap went through the stop, so check the report date before you look at the chart.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: What did the close tell you?
choices: A failed breakout; the stop decides
A normal pause; add on the dip
A shakeout; move the stop lower
Too early to tell; wait for a new day
questions.answer: A failed breakout; the stop decides
questions.why: A failed breakout. A breakout that closes back inside the base in the lower third of its day's range is a failed breakout. QCOM closed at the low of its range, 183.32, back inside the base. Let the stop decide, which is the default, or sell on that close. The next session's low, 179.41, took the 183.06 stop.
questions.lesson_line: A close back inside the base at the low means the stop decides.

wrong.A normal pause; add on the dip: No adds. A close at the low back inside the base is a warning.
wrong.A shakeout; move the stop lower: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Too early to tell; wait for a new day: The test is the close, and it already failed: the close was at the low of its range, back inside the base.

questions.story: QCOM, 2021. A 26-session base breaks out and you buy at 188.78. The day closes at the low of its range, back inside the base.
questions.simple: It was a failed breakout, since it closed back inside the base at the low, so the stop decides.

deeper.trap: The test is the close, not an intraday dip. A breakout that dips into the base and then closes in the upper part of its range does not fail this test. QCOM closed at the low of its range, 183.32, back inside the base, so it did.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)
failed-breakout test is a proposed card line

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Move the stop lower, the base is sound
Take the stop; re-enter on new trigger
Buy again at once, same stop
Hold; the dip under the stop was a wick

After a stop-out you buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. The stop only moves up, so lowering it breaks the rule, and a real stop order has already sold it.
questions.lesson_line: A valid base can still fail. The stop pays for that.

wrong.Move the stop lower, the base is sound: The stop only moves up. A stop moved down breaks the rule.
wrong.Buy again at once, same stop: After a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.
wrong.Hold; the dip under the stop was a wick: The stop is the exit. A real stop order with the broker has already sold it when price traded under 59.88.

questions.story: OXY, 2022. A valid 16-session base after a 62% run breaks out. You buy at 62.10 with the stop at 59.88. The next day's low is 59.83.
questions.simple: Take the stop, because a valid base can still fail and the stop is there for that.

deeper.trap: A valid setup can still fail. OXY's base passed its tests and the stock fell through the stop the next day. In our research scan, 28.9% reached 3R and 20.0% reached 5R before the stop, and 92% were eventually stopped within 60 sessions. A stop-out is part of the cost of the setup, not proof you were wrong.

A Wedge Pop after a long decline
A bull flag, the rest is too short
An EMA Crossback; a dip to a line

wrong.A Wedge Pop after a long decline: A Wedge Pop comes from under the averages after a decline, not from a short rest.
wrong.An EMA Crossback; a dip to a line: A Crossback is a first dip into the rising 10 or 20 EMA. This stock rested sideways.

questions.story: NVDA, 2024. A 39% run, then the stock rests only 8 sessions sideways before it breaks out.

deeper.trap: Eight sessions feels close to ten, but the card draws a hard line: the breakout rests 10 to 40 sessions, and under 10 sessions the rest is a flag. A bull flag is its own setup, a 3 to 15-session drift after a 20% pole.

The base length of 19 sessions
The size of the run before the base
Lighter volume late in the base

questions.q: Which check fails?

Closes above the rising 20-day
The depth cap of 25% or less
Closes above the rising 50-day line

Pass; the base is too short to trust
Take it; rising lows, tight finish
Take it; the base runs 45 sessions

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before a possible breakout. Is this a clean base to buy? Take it or pass.
choices: Pass; the box makes a lower low
