questions.lesson_line: Never own more than 1% of average daily volume.
questions.simple: One percent of the average daily volume is 8,000 shares, which is less than 12,000, so 8,000 is the limit.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: Our size cap is 1% of today's volume, so a heavy day lifts it.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The cap is 1% of average daily volume, so one heavy day does not lift it. You never own more than that, and illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: Size to 1% of average volume, never today's.
questions.simple: False, because the cap uses the average daily volume, so one busy day cannot raise it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: Our card calls which base depth the A+ depth?
choices: 15% deep or less
25% deep or less
Half the prior move or less
10% deep or less
questions.answer: 15% deep or less
questions.why: 15% deep or less. A consolidation 15% deep or less is the A+ depth on our card. The cap that decides whether a base counts at all is 25% or less, and also no more than half of the prior move. A base between 15% and 25% still counts but is not the A+ depth.
questions.lesson_line: A base 15% deep or less is the A+ depth.

wrong.25% deep or less: That is the cap every base must pass, not the A+ line.
wrong.Half the prior move or less: That is the second depth cap. A base can pass it and still not be A+ depth.
wrong.10% deep or less: The A+ depth is 15% or less. Ten percent is not a line on the card.

questions.simple: A base 15% deep or less is the A+ depth, while 25% is only the cap every base must pass.

reasons: Both depth lines are the card's proposed numbers
The 25% cap awaits an owner ruling

questions.q: Which breakout has the better depth?
choices: The 12% base; it is the shallower one
The 23% base; it has more room to run
Equal; any base under the cap is alike
Neither; depth plays no part in grading
questions.answer: The 12% base; it is the shallower one
questions.why: The 12% base. Both pass the 25% cap, but only the 12% base is inside the 15% A+ depth. Depth is one cue among several, and grading is discretionary and hard to define.
questions.lesson_line: Shallow and tight earns the A+ depth.

wrong.Equal; any base under the cap is alike: Both pass the cap, but on our card 15% or less is the A+ depth.
wrong.The 23% base; it has more room to run: Deeper is not better. It only has to stay under the 25% cap; 15% or less earns the A+ depth.
wrong.Neither; depth plays no part in grading: Depth is a cue. On our card, 15% or less is the A+ depth.

questions.story: Two leaders break out of 15-session bases after similar runs. One base is 12% deep and the other is 23% deep. Both pass the cap.
questions.simple: The 12 percent base is better, because it is shallower and inside the 15 percent A+ depth.

reasons: rests on the criteria card, which the owner has not yet ruled on
grading is a judgment call

questions.q: Does the breakout day pass our card?
choices: No; the averages show no up cycle
No; the base needs 25 sessions or more
Yes; the base and volume are enough
Yes; flat averages show a tight base
questions.answer: No; the averages show no up cycle
questions.why: No. On the breakout day our card needs the 10-day EMA above the 20-day EMA, with both rising. That is an up cycle. Here the 10 is under the 20 and both are flat, so it fails even though the base and volume look fine. Volume only raises the grade. Kell sees no reason to be long with the 10-day EMA under the 20-day.
questions.lesson_line: Breakout day: the 10 over the 20, both rising.

wrong.Yes; the base and volume are enough: The card also asks for the 10-day EMA above the 20-day EMA, both rising.
wrong.No; the base needs 25 sessions or more: The base runs 10 to 40 sessions, so 20 fits.
wrong.Yes; flat averages show a tight base: Flat averages fail the test. Both lines must be rising.

questions.story: A leader breaks out of a 20-session base on good volume. It closes above its 50-day and 200-day, and the 50 is above the 200. Its 10-day EMA sits just under the 20-day EMA, and both are flat.
questions.simple: No, because the 10-day average must sit above the 20-day, with both rising, and here it sits under and both are flat.

deeper.counter: A long base and good volume do not rescue a bad order of the averages. The check reads the breakout day itself, and volume only raises the grade. A 10 under the 20 means no up cycle yet, and no longs in a down cycle.

reasons: Uses the 10/20 EMA pair held by D-021
Card rule on the breakout day
Fixed before

questions.q: What do you set up tonight?
choices: An alert at the high; the plan written
A limit order resting at the base high
Nothing yet; you decide after the open
An after-hours buy just under the high
questions.answer: An alert at the high; the plan written
questions.why: An alert at the base high and a written plan. The buy itself is a market order when the level breaks, in regular hours only. Entry, stop and size are written down before the market opens. A limit order resting at the high is not our entry, and nothing is bought after hours.
questions.lesson_line: Alert the night before, then a market order.

wrong.A limit order resting at the base high: Our entries are market orders, bought as the level breaks.
wrong.Nothing yet; you decide after the open: The entry, stop and size are written before the market opens.
wrong.An after-hours buy just under the high: No new buys outside regular trading hours. The buy waits for the level to break tomorrow.

questions.story: It is 6 pm. A leader sits just under its base high, and you plan to buy the break tomorrow.
questions.simple: Set an alert at the base high tonight and write your plan, then buy at market when it breaks.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58, D39)

questions.q: If a leader breaks its level in pre-market, we buy it there with a market order.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Entries are market orders, but no new buys go in outside regular trading hours. A pre-market break waits for regular hours, and if it is then more than 4% above the trigger we skip it.
questions.lesson_line: Market order, regular hours. Pre-market breaks wait.
questions.simple: False, because we buy only in regular hours, so a pre-market break has to wait.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: The 10-day average is 50.00. At what price does a long become too stretched to buy?
questions.why: 55.00. Ten percent above 50.00 is 55.00. We skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average, so a price above 55.00 is skipped.
questions.lesson_line: Skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day.
questions.simple: Add ten percent of the 10-day average to itself, and any price above that is too stretched to buy.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: Buy at market, or pass? Choose the call and the reason.
choices: Pass; over 10% above its 10-day
Buy; it is inside 4% of the high
Buy half now and half on a dip
Pass; 3% over the high is too far
questions.answer: Pass; over 10% above its 10-day
questions.why: Pass. It is within 4% of the base high, so the chase test passes. But 41.20 is more than 10% above the 36.00 average, so the stretch test fails.
questions.lesson_line: Two checks: under 4% past the high, and under 10% stretched.

wrong.Buy; it is inside 4% of the high: That test passes, but the stretch test fails. Both apply.
wrong.Buy half now and half on a dip: No scaling. A stock this stretched is skipped.
wrong.Pass; 3% over the high is too far: 3% is inside the 4% limit, so the chase test passes. The stretch test is what fails.

questions.story: The base high is 40.00. After a run, the stock opens at 41.20, just 3% over it. Its 10-day average is 36.00.
questions.simple: Pass, because the stock is more than 10 percent above its 10-day average, even though it is near the high.

deeper.trap: Both lines must pass. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. This open is 3% over the high but far over the average, so the second line fails.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook
the key needs a little arithmetic

questions.q: May you buy it?
choices: Yes, as a new trade with its own stop
Yes, but only with half the usual size
No; a missed breakout is gone for good
Yes, and keep the stop from Monday
questions.answer: Yes, as a new trade with its own stop
questions.why: Yes, as a new trade. A missed breakout that returns to its level may be bought as a new trade, with its own trigger and stop. Kullamagi says he sometimes buys the retrace. The 4% chase limit still applies.
questions.lesson_line: A retrace buy is a new trade with its own stop.

wrong.No; a missed breakout is gone for good: Kullamagi sometimes buys the retrace, so a miss is not final.
wrong.Yes, but only with half the usual size: Size comes from the stop and the risk rule. Missing the first move does not halve it.
wrong.Yes, and keep the stop from Monday: A retrace buy is a new trade with its own trigger and stop, not Monday's.

questions.story: A leader broke out Monday and you missed it. By Thursday it dips back to the old base high and turns up through it.
questions.simple: Yes, you may buy it as a new trade with its own trigger and stop.

deeper.trap: A retrace buy is a second chance, not a bargain. It needs its own trigger, its own stop and the 4% limit, and the size comes from the new stop. The first breakout's stop and size do not carry over.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook
the Kullamagi view comes from a reply in his comments

questions.q: You bought at 50.00 with the stop at 48.00. A gap-down day's first 30-minute low is 45.80. What is the loss, in R?
questions.why: 2.1R. One R is the buy minus the stop, 50.00 minus 48.00. The first 30-minute low of 45.80 is 2.1 times that far under the buy. That is past the 2R ceiling, so you get out.
questions.lesson_line: First 30 minutes past 2R: get out.
questions.simple: The loss at the 30 minute low is 2.1 times your risk, which is past 2R, so you get out.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: Where does your stop go now?
choices: 47.20, the first 30-minute low
48.00; the old stop still stands
Sell at the open, whatever the price
46.00, a stop 2R under your buy
questions.answer: 47.20, the first 30-minute low
questions.why: 47.20. After a gap against the stop, the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of that first 30-minute bar is the new stop. The stock opened at 47.60, under the old 48.00 stop, so the old stop cannot hold. At 47.20 the loss stays inside 2R, so you do not have to get out. If the first 30 minutes took the loss past 2R, you would.
questions.lesson_line: After a gap, the first 30-minute low is the stop.

wrong.48.00; the old stop still stands: The stop sits above the open, so it cannot hold. The first 30 minutes set the new one.
wrong.Sell at the open, whatever the price: You get out only if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R. Here they do not.
wrong.46.00, a stop 2R under your buy: 2R under 50.00 is 46.00. That is the ceiling: past it you get out. It is not the new stop.

questions.story: You bought at 50.00 with the stop at 48.00. The stock gaps open at 47.60. The first 30-minute low is 47.20.
questions.simple: Use 47.20, the low of the first 30-minute bar, as the new stop, because the gap went through the old one.

deeper.trap: Selling at the open feels safe, but it is not the rule. The rule waits for the first 30-minute bar, then sets the stop at its low. You get out only if that low takes the loss past 2R of the original risk.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 gap rule)
The 2R test is computed from the entry and old stop

questions.q: Is that enough?
choices: No; enter a real stop with the broker
Yes; you are watching the screen anyway
Partly; add a price alert as a backup
No; add the stop after the first win
questions.answer: No; enter a real stop with the broker
questions.why: No. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. Watching the screen does not replace the order, and a price alert is not an order. The stop also comes first, before the size.
questions.lesson_line: A real stop order, placed with the broker.

wrong.Yes; you are watching the screen anyway: A stop kept in your head is not a stop. Every position has a real order.
wrong.Partly; add a price alert as a backup: An alert is not an order. The stop sits with the broker.
wrong.No; add the stop after the first win: Stop first. Our rule sets the stop before the size, so it cannot wait for a win.

questions.story: You will be at your screen all day. You plan to sell by hand if the stock falls to your stop.
questions.simple: No, a stop kept in your head is not a stop, so the real order must sit with the broker.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: After the buy, you may lower the stop a little to give the trade room.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule, a fixed procedure after a gap against the stop.
questions.lesson_line: A stop moves up. It does not widen.
questions.simple: False, because once set the stop only moves up, never down or wider.

deeper.trap: The pull is to lower the stop just this once when the trade dips near it. But moving it down or wider breaks the rule. A gap is the only exception, and it follows a fixed procedure, not a mood.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: Ideally, at what gain does our rulebook move the stop up to breakeven?
choices: Between 2R and 5R
Between 6R and 10R
Between 0R and 1R
Between 10R and 20R
questions.answer: Between 2R and 5R
questions.why: Between 2R and 5R. Our rulebook says to move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The card sets it at the first trim by default. It is a guide, not a hard rule.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R.

wrong.Between 0R and 1R: That is before the window. The ideal is 2R to 5R.
wrong.Between 10R and 20R: That is far past the window. The ideal is 2R to 5R.
wrong.Between 6R and 10R: That is past the window. The ideal is 2R to 5R.

questions.simple: Between 2R and 5R of profit, and by default when you take the first trim.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook
the breakeven window is an ideal, not a hard rule

questions.q: Bought at 36.00 with the stop at 34.00. At what price does the ideal breakeven window open?
questions.why: 40.00. One R is the buy minus the stop, which is 36.00 minus 34.00. The window opens at 2R, so 40.00. From there the stop may move up to the 36.00 entry, ideally anywhere from 2R to 5R.
questions.lesson_line: 2R above the buy opens the breakeven window.
questions.simple: At 2R the price is the buy plus two times the risk, so the stop may then move up to breakeven.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: Bought at 52.35 with the stop at 51.21. Where is 5R, the second trim?
questions.why: 58.05. One R is the buy minus the stop, 52.35 minus 51.21. Five R above the buy is 58.05. Another third comes off there, after the first third at 3R. The ladder is adjustable.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, trail the rest.
questions.simple: One R is the buy minus the stop, so add five of those to the buy to find 5R.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: How many shares do you sell?
choices: Another 300; trail the final 300
All 600 now, because 5R is plenty
Nothing; wait for 10R before trimming
Sell 200, a third of what is left
questions.answer: Another 300; trail the final 300
questions.why: Another 300, then trail the final 300. You bought 900 shares and sold a third at 3R, so 600 are left. At 5R the plan sells another third, 300 here, and trails the last third. The levels can be adjusted, but the shape is a third, a third, then a trail.
questions.lesson_line: At 5R, sell the second third.

wrong.All 600 now, because 5R is plenty: Our plan sells a third at 5R and trails the rest, so winners can run.
wrong.Nothing; wait for 10R before trimming: The second trim comes at 5R. Waiting longer skips it.
wrong.Sell 200, a third of what is left: That leaves more than a third to trail. The plan sells another third, 300 here, and trails the last third.

questions.story: You bought 900 shares and sold a third at 3R. The stock now reaches 5R.
questions.simple: Sell another 300 shares, a third of the position, and trail the last 300.

deeper.example: Walk it through. 900 shares. A third, 300, goes at 3R, leaving 600. Another 300 goes at 5R, leaving 300. That last 300 trails: a close under the 10-day for a fast mover, or under the 21-day for a steadier one, is the sale.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, adjustable)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: If a stock gaps above a trim level (3R or 5R), take that trim at the ___.
questions.answer: open
questions.why: Open. A stock that gaps above a trim level (3R or 5R) is already past it. You take that trim at the open, not at a pullback or a later dip.
questions.lesson_line: Gap above a trim level: take it at the open.
questions.simple: If a stock gaps above a trim level, you sell that trim at the open, not later.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)

questions.q: When do you take the first third?
choices: At once; it is already past 46.00
Wait for a dip back down to 46.00
Hold until 5R, since it gapped up
Sell the whole position at the open
questions.answer: At once; it is already past 46.00
questions.why: At the open. The stock opened at 47.50, above the 46.00 trim level, so you take that trim at the open. The first trim is a third at 3R. The rest stays on for the next trim and the trail.
questions.lesson_line: Opens past the level: take the trim now.

wrong.Wait for a dip back down to 46.00: Waiting risks giving the gain back. The level is already passed.
wrong.Hold until 5R, since it gapped up: The first trim is a third at 3R, and the gap only means you take it sooner.
wrong.Sell the whole position at the open: The first trim is only a third at 3R. The rest stays on for the next trim and the trail.

questions.story: You bought at 40.00 with the stop at 38.00, so 3R is 46.00. The next morning the stock opens at 47.50.
questions.simple: The stock opened above the trim level, so you sell the first third right at the open.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Sell it now and free the money
Hold; the stop has not been hit
Move the stop to breakeven, wait
Sell half now and hold the rest
questions.answer: Sell it now and free the money
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. The stop has not been hit, but the time stop is a second exit. Breakeven is for a winner: the stop ideally moves there between 2R and 5R, so at 0.4R it is too early.
questions.lesson_line: Under 1R after 10 trading days: sell.

wrong.Hold; the stop has not been hit: The time stop is a second exit. A stalled trade does not wait for the stop.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven, wait: A stalled trade is sold. The stop ideally moves to breakeven between 2R and 5R, not at 0.4R.
wrong.Sell half now and hold the rest: The time stop sells the trade, not half of it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

questions.story: You bought a breakout 10 trading days ago. It has chopped sideways and is up 0.4R. The stop was never touched.
questions.simple: Sell it, because a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold to free the money.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: A trade up 1.5R after ten trading days still has to be sold by the time stop.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The time stop sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days. At 1.5R the trade is working, so it stays. The stop still protects it, and the trims at 3R and 5R still apply.
questions.lesson_line: The time stop is for trades stuck under 1R.
questions.simple: False, because the time stop only sells a trade that is still under 1R after 10 trading days.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: What do you do with the position?
choices: Sell a big part into the burst
Add; it is working best right now
Hold it all and wait for the 10-day
Trim a small piece, hold the rest
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the burst
questions.why: Sell a big part into the burst. The story shows four signs of a parabolic burst, a 3-5 day final leg: three straight up days, two overnight gap ups, two days of rising volume, and a gap up on the climax day. It is a judgment call, so the exact amount is yours, but the rule says a big part, not a token trim. The rest trails.
questions.lesson_line: A climax run is a time to sell strength.

wrong.Add; it is working best right now: A climax is where you take profit, not where you add.
wrong.Hold it all and wait for the 10-day: The rule says sell a big part into the burst. The trail comes after.
wrong.Trim a small piece, hold the rest: The rule is to sell a big part into a climax, not a token amount.

questions.story: Your long has jumped three straight days with two overnight gaps up. Volume rose two days running, and today it gaps up again.
questions.simple: Sell a big part into the burst, because a climax run is a time to sell into strength.

deeper.trap: Adding feels right because the stock is working best right now. But a climax is the moment the move is most stretched, and the rule is to sell a big part into it, not add. The rest still trails: a close under the 10-day for a fast mover, or under the 21-day for a steadier one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, B26)
a judgment call by the owner's own words

questions.q: Which sign belongs to a parabolic burst?
choices: Two straight overnight gap ups
Volume shrinking on each up day
Three tight inside days in a row
A single gap up, then a quiet week
questions.answer: Two straight overnight gap ups
questions.why: Two straight overnight gap ups. A parabolic burst is a 3-5 day final leg: three straight up days, two straight overnight gap ups, two of three days of range expansion, two days of rising volume, and a gap up on the climax day.
questions.lesson_line: A burst: gaps, wide ranges, rising volume.

wrong.Volume shrinking on each up day: A burst runs on rising volume, not falling volume.
wrong.Three tight inside days in a row: A burst widens its ranges. Tight inside days are the opposite.
wrong.A single gap up, then a quiet week: A burst has two straight overnight gap ups, with wide ranges and rising volume. One gap and calm is not it.

questions.simple: A parabolic burst has gaps, wide ranges and rising volume, so two straight gap ups fit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: After the buy, what ends a trade that is not working?
choices: Either the stop or the time stop
A red close right after the buy
A hunch that the market is weak
Lowering the stop to wait it out
questions.answer: Either the stop or the time stop
questions.why: The stop, or the time stop. After the buy the stop is the exit, and it only moves up. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, which frees the money.
questions.lesson_line: After the buy: the stop, or the time stop.

wrong.A hunch that the market is weak: A hunch is not a rule. After the buy, the stop is the exit.
wrong.A red close right after the buy: One red close is not an exit. After the buy, the stop is the exit.
wrong.Lowering the stop to wait it out: The stop only moves up, never down or wider. Lowering it breaks the rule.

questions.simple: The stop ends a losing trade, and the time stop sells one still under 1R after 10 days.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Hold; the stop is still the exit
Sell at the open; the news is bad
Lower the stop to ride out the dip
Add on the dip; the news is noise
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is still the exit
questions.why: Hold. The stop is the exit, so a headline does not change the plan while the stop holds. The stock is still above the stop and in profit. The stop only moves up, and the full size was bought at one price with one stop, so there is no add.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the exit. News is not.

wrong.Sell at the open; the news is bad: The stop is the exit. A headline does not change the plan while the stop holds.
wrong.Add on the dip; the news is noise: No adds. It is one price with one stop, and the stop is the exit.

questions.story: Day 6 after the buy. An analyst downgrade opens the stock down 2%. It is still above your stop and still in profit.
questions.simple: Hold, because the stop is the exit and a headline does not change the plan.

deeper.trap: A downgrade feels like new information, so selling or adding feels smart. But the plan was set before the buy, with a real stop order at the broker. Overriding it on a headline swaps a rule for a mood. If the stock gaps through the stop, a different rule applies: the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop, and you are out if the loss passes 2R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, A5)

questions.q: What sets up a Wedge Pop?
choices: A drop, then price and EMAs tighten
A flat base riding above both the EMAs
A first dip into the rising 20 EMA
Three straight gap ups on volume
questions.answer: A drop, then price and EMAs tighten
questions.why: A drop, then a squeeze. A Wedge Pop follows a Reversal Extension or a correction of 15% or more. Price then tightens under or against the 10/20 EMA for at least 3 sessions while the two averages converge. A cross of the averages alone is not the setup.
questions.lesson_line: Fall, then tighten: that is the Wedge Pop setting.

wrong.A flat base riding above both the EMAs: That is the base behind a Qullamaggie breakout, which surfs above the rising averages. A Wedge Pop comes from under them.
wrong.A first dip into the rising 20 EMA: That is the EMA Crossback, the first pullback after the pop.
wrong.Three straight gap ups on volume: Gaps up with no squeeze first are not a wedge. A Wedge Pop needs the tight, converging range before the break.

questions.simple: Price falls first, then it squeezes tight against the averages while they move together, and that squeeze sets up the pop.

reasons: Numbers (15%, 3 sessions) from the card's proposed Wedge Pop setting
Uses the 10/20 EMA pair held by D-021

questions.q: Kell skips the first 10 to 15 minutes of the session unless a stock has a catalyst like earnings.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Kell says he does not trade the first 10-15 minutes unless a stock has a catalyst like earnings. We have no time-of-day rule, so this is his habit, not ours.
questions.lesson_line: Kell waits 10-15 minutes. For us it is not a rule.
questions.simple: True, Kell waits 10 to 15 minutes at the open unless there is news like earnings, but we have no such rule.

reasons: rests on one web source for Kell's habit (L19)
rests on the owner's rulebook (C30)

questions.q: Does the early hour alone stop you from buying under our rulebook?
choices: No; we have no time-of-day rule
Yes; Kell's wait is our rule too
Only if there is news that day
No; but wait for the 30-minute bar
questions.answer: No; we have no time-of-day rule
questions.why: No. We have no time-of-day rule, so a break at 9:36 is not blocked by the clock. Kell does not trade the first 10-15 minutes unless a stock has a catalyst. That is his habit, not our rule.
questions.lesson_line: No time rule. Kell's wait is his habit, not ours.

wrong.Yes; Kell's wait is our rule too: Kell's wait is his habit. Our rulebook has no time-of-day rule.
wrong.Only if there is news that day: We have no time-of-day rule, with or without news.
wrong.No; but wait for the 30-minute bar: The first 30-minute bar only sets a new stop after a gap against a stop. It is not a wait to buy.

questions.story: A leader trades through its pivot at 9:36, six minutes after the open, on no news. Kell would wait 10 to 15 minutes without a catalyst.

questions.q: Where does the EMA Crossback stop go?
choices: A few cents under the pullback's low
A few cents under the 50-day average
Two ATRs under the pullback's low
Just under the prior session's high
questions.answer: A few cents under the pullback's low
questions.why: A few cents under the pullback's low. Kell uses the low against the 10 or 20 EMA as his stop when he buys off support. The trigger is a trade above the prior session's high, and the stop sits a few cents under the pullback's low, not exactly on it.
questions.lesson_line: Crossback stop: under the pullback's low.

wrong.Two ATRs under the pullback's low: The stop is the low itself, a few cents under, not a volatility multiple.
wrong.Just under the prior session's high: The prior high is the trigger, not the stop.
wrong.A few cents under the 50-day average: Nothing in the Crossback stop uses the 50-day. The stop is set from the pullback's low.

questions.simple: Put the stop a few cents under the low of the pullback, not under the prior high.

questions.q: Kell might size a 15% position with a 2% stop. What share of the account does that risk, in percent?

questions.lesson_line: Position size times stop width is the risk.
questions.simple: Risk is the position size times the stop width, so 15% times 2% is 0.3% of the account.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Buy at market; it is past the pivot
Wait for a dip back to the 20 EMA
Buy tomorrow, after a close above it
Skip it; the base needs 10 sessions
questions.answer: Buy at market; it is past the pivot
questions.why: Buy at market. A Base n' Break buys as price trades through the pivot into new highs, and our entries are market orders. The 8-session shelf fits a tight base of 5 to 15 sessions holding the rising averages.
questions.lesson_line: Base n' Break: through the pivot, at market.

wrong.Wait for a dip back to the 20 EMA: A dip to the 20 EMA is the Crossback, a different phase.
wrong.Buy tomorrow, after a close above it: The buy area is through the pivot. Buying tomorrow adds distance.
wrong.Skip it; the base needs 10 sessions: That is the breakout's base length. A Base n' Break is a tight base of 5 to 15 sessions.

questions.story: A leader in an up cycle holds a tight 8-session shelf on its rising 10 EMA, near its highs. You treat it as a Base n' Break. Today it trades through the shelf's high to a new high.
questions.simple: Buy at market right as it trades through the top of the shelf to a new high.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: Where does the stop go?
choices: A few cents under 49.10, breakout low
A few cents under 48.20, the pivot low
At 50.30, the buy price, at once
A mental stop at 49.10, no order placed
questions.answer: A few cents under 49.10, breakout low
questions.why: A few cents under 49.10. A Base n' Break stop goes a few cents under the low of the pivot bar or the breakout day. Take whichever is closer and honest. Both lows here are honest, so the closer one wins. Stops below those lows let you ride the averages higher. The stop is a real order with the broker, and it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Base n' Break stop: the closer honest low.

wrong.A few cents under 48.20, the pivot low: Both lows are honest, so take the closer one. 48.20 only adds distance.
wrong.At 50.30, the buy price, at once: A stop at the buy gives the trade no room. The stop moves to breakeven between 2R and 5R.
wrong.A mental stop at 49.10, no order placed: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.

questions.story: You buy a Base n' Break at 50.30. The pivot bar's low is 48.20 and the breakout day's low is 49.10. Both are honest levels.
questions.simple: Put the stop a few cents under 49.10, the closer of the two honest lows, so you risk less.

deeper.trap: The wider stop at 48.20 can look safer, but it is not. The size comes from the stop, so a wider stop means a smaller position. When both lows are honest, the card takes the closer one.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (D41 real stop order, A4)

questions.q: Do you add?
choices: No; one price, one stop, no adding
Yes; Kell treats it as an addition
No; wait and add on the next dip
Yes; the stock earned a bigger size
questions.answer: No; one price, one stop, no adding
questions.why: No. Kell calls the Base n' Break an addition to leading stocks. Our rule is full size at one price with one stop, no adding. A later phase is a new trade from flat, with its own stop and size.
questions.lesson_line: No adds. A later phase is a new trade from flat.

wrong.Yes; Kell treats it as an addition: Kell calls the Base n' Break an addition. Our rule is full size at one price with one stop.
wrong.No; wait and add on the next dip: We do not add. A later phase is its own trade from flat, not an add on a dip.
wrong.Yes; the stock earned a bigger size: No adding: the full size goes in at one price with one stop. A bigger size is also an add.

questions.story: You hold a leader bought at its Wedge Pop. It now breaks out of its first Base n' Break, and a friend quotes Kell and says to add shares.
questions.simple: No, we never add. Kell calls it an addition, but our rule is one price and one stop.

deeper.trap: Kell's own article calls the Base n' Break an addition to leading stocks. A member who reads him will see the word add. We teach our rule instead: one price, one stop, no adding. A later Base n' Break is a new trade from flat, with its own stop and size.

questions.q: What is a parabolic long, our one exception to the rule on longs below the long-term average?
choices: A burst down, the mirror image
A burst up, with gaps and volume
A slow drift up above its averages
A first dip into the rising 20-day
questions.answer: A burst down, the mirror image
questions.why: A burst down. We take no longs below the 200-day simple average, unless it is a parabolic long. Our parabolic long is the mirror image of the burst up: a burst down.
questions.simple: A parabolic long is a burst down, the mirror of the burst up. It is the one long allowed under the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: The 200-day exception is a parabolic long: a burst down.

wrong.A burst up, with gaps and volume: That is the burst up, the signs of a climax run. Our parabolic long is its mirror image, a burst down.
wrong.A first dip into the rising 20-day: A first dip into the rising 20 EMA is a Crossback, a different setup. The exception is a parabolic long, a burst down.
wrong.A slow drift up above its averages: A long already above the average needs no exception. The exception covers longs below it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: With the breakout level at 77.67, a buy at 81.20 breaks our rule against chasing.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point. A buy at 81.20 is past that limit above 77.67, so it is a chase.
questions.simple: True, because 81.20 is more than 4% above the 77.67 breakout level.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% above the breakout level is a chase.

deeper.counter: Passing today is not a ban on the stock. A missed breakout that comes back to the breakout level may be bought as a new trade with its own trigger and stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
